explicacion.es: «¿no?» es un calco del español. La tag copia el auxiliar con polaridad contraria: have → haven't you?

texto.es: En una charla informal, el inglés casi nunca contesta con un simple «yes» o «no»: devuelve un eco. El eco repite el auxiliar de la frase, con su pronombre y con la misma polaridad (I've joined… → Have you?; She didn't call → Didn't she?). No pide información: muestra interés o sorpresa, y suele ir seguido de una pregunta. No lo confundas con la question tag (You've met him, haven't you?), que tiene polaridad contraria y pide confirmar lo que ya crees. Otras fichas: Fair enough, No way!, Guess what?
Afirmación + eco + pregunta:

nota.es: afirmación con auxiliar (have)
eco: mismo auxiliar + pronombre; muestra interés
pregunta breve que mantiene viva la charla

titulo.es: Cabeza y cola en la charla oral

texto.es: En la conversación oral, el inglés saca el tema de la frase. Con la cabeza (head) el tema va primero y un pronombre lo retoma: My brother, he's a cook. Con la cola (tail) la frase completa va primero y el tema se añade al final: He's a cook, my brother. En español puedes omitir el sujeto; en inglés el pronombre es obligatorio y concuerda con el nombre (sister → she, neighbours → they, film → it). Son recursos del habla informal: en un texto formal no se usan.
Cabeza + pronombre + comentario:

nota.es: cabeza: el tema de la charla
pronombre obligatorio que retoma el tema
comentario sobre el tema

titulo.es: Réplicas cortas: lo omitido y lo sustituido

texto.es: Cuando contestas rápido, no repites lo que el otro ya dijo. Hay tres recursos. Uno: dejar solo to (I'd love to = I'd love to come). Dos: So/Neither + auxiliar + sujeto para «yo también / yo tampoco»; el auxiliar copia el de la frase original (am, do, did, have, can…). Tres: sustituir la oración entera con so o not (I hope so, I think so, I hope not, I'm afraid not). Para entender una réplica, busca el auxiliar y reconstruye el verbo que falta en la frase anterior.
Frase + réplica elíptica:

nota.es: frase original con el auxiliar didn't
yo tampoco (se usa tras una frase negativa)
auxiliar copiado + sujeto nuevo; el verbo se omite

texto.es: Los marcadores de discurso guían la conversación y suelen ir al inicio de la réplica, seguidos de coma. By the way y speaking of… cambian de tema (el primero, algo que se te ocurre; el segundo, enlazando con lo dicho). Anyway vuelve al tema principal. To be honest da una opinión sincera sin sonar brusco. Come to think of it marca un recuerdo repentino. Actually corrige o matiza con cortesía: ¡no significa «actualmente»! Usa pocos y variados: si los repites en cada frase, suenas ensayado.
Marcador + coma + idea:

nota.es: marcador: abre un tema nuevo
la pregunta o idea nueva
el resto de la frase es normal

titulo.es: La sobremesa: los cuatro recursos juntos

texto.es: En una sobremesa se combinan los recursos de la charla informal: ecos para reaccionar (Is she? Did he?), cabeza o cola para hablar de alguien (My sister, she's…; She's lovely, your sister), elipsis para acordar o rechazar (Neither can I, I'd love to, I'd rather not) y marcadores para dirigir el rumbo (By the way, Anyway, To be honest). Propón un tema, reacciona a lo que dicen los demás y cambia de tema con un marcador. Si solo hablas tú, no es una conversación.
Tema + reacción + cambio de tema:

nota.es: marcador + cabeza: propones el tema

formula.texto: "Is she? I'd love to try it."

nota.es: eco + elipsis: reaccionas al comentario
marcador: cambias o vuelves al plan

texto.es: En la narrativa, el inglés altera el orden normal para dar ritmo. Anteposición de lugar: Down the hill ran the dog; si el sujeto es un nombre, el verbo va antes (ran the dog), pero con pronombre no hay inversión (Down the hill it ran). Un adverbio negativo al inicio pide auxiliar + sujeto: Never had she seen such a view. Los fragmentos sin verbo (Silence. Then footsteps.) crean tensión. Alterna frases largas con una corta que golpea. Son recursos literarios: si los usas en cada frase, pierden efecto.

titulo.es: Saltos en el tiempo de una anécdota

texto.es: Una anécdota casi nunca va en orden. La línea principal se cuenta en pasado simple (arrived, gave, talked). Lo anterior va en pasado perfecto (had promised, had told) y lo que ya duraba antes de un hecho, en pasado perfecto continuo (had been waiting). Lo posterior, visto desde el pasado, con would + verbo (she would marry him). Los marcadores ayudan: years earlier, by the time, three years later. Para reconstruir el orden real, ordena por tiempo verbal y marcadores, no por el orden en que aparece cada frase.
Hecho principal + fondo anterior:

nota.es: hecho principal en past simple
fondo anterior: past perfect continuous
duración hasta ese momento

texto.es: Una anécdota con giro tiene tres partes. Escena: el fondo en pasado continuo con detalles (The rain was tapping on the windows). Hecho y giro: algo la rompe en pasado simple (Suddenly, a woman sat down), a menudo con una intención que no se cumple o una acción interrumpida: I was about to pay when… / I was going to call the police, but then… Desenlace: se anticipa con would, y tras little se invierte: Little did I know that she would become my partner. Sigue el orden escena → hecho → giro → desenlace.

Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My uncle Tom would always tell the same story about his first car. That year, he was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my grandmother laughed and opened her arms. "It's Leo!" she said. He had been travelling for ten years, and nobody had known where he was. Little did we know that he would stay with us for the whole summer.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your uncle say? Fair enough, he said. Tonight, for once, we'll hear a new story.

titulo.es: Contar la anécdota en la reunión

texto.es: Contar una anécdota en una reunión junta todo lo aprendido. Abre con un hábito o una escena mostrada (At every reunion, my uncle would…; The kitchen smelled of coffee…). Rompe la escena con un hecho en past simple o con was about to; da el giro mirando hacia atrás (had been planning) y anticipa el final con Little did I know… + would. Cierra con una frase corta o un fragmento (Silence. Then laughter.). Después, responde al público con naturalidad: un eco, un marcador (Anyway, To be honest) y respuestas cortas.

nota.es: giro mirando atrás y desenlace anticipado

items.respuesta:
Every summer, the whole family used to meet at my grandmother's house. The kitchen smelled of coffee, and the relatives were all talking at once. My uncle Tom would always tell the same story about his first car. That year, he was about to start it again when a stranger walked into the garden. Nobody recognised him. Silence. Then my grandmother laughed and opened her arms. "It's Leo!" she said. He had been travelling for ten years, and nobody had known where he was. Little did we know that he would stay with us for the whole summer.
Did you recognise him? No, I didn't. I thought he was a neighbour.
What did your uncle say? Fair enough, he said. Tonight, for once, we'll hear a new story.

texto.es: En español también decimos «¡Qué bien!» cuando algo sale mal. En inglés hay dos trucos parecidos: la ironía (dices lo contrario: «Lovely weather!» bajo la lluvia) y el understatement, muy típico del inglés británico (dices menos de lo que pasa: «a bit of a disaster» cuando el techo se ha caído). Para reconocerlos, compara lo que se dice con la situación: si no coinciden, hay intención; si coinciden, la frase es literal. Como el audio no muestra el tono, busca la pista en el contexto.
Lo que se dice + lo que ocurre = intención:

nota.es: lo que se dice: palabras positivas
lo que ocurre: una situación mala
intención: ironía, dice lo contrario

titulo.es: Juegos de palabras: una palabra, dos sentidos

texto.es: Un juego de palabras (pun) aprovecha que una palabra tiene dos sentidos (double meaning) o que suena igual que otra (homophone). Primero preparas un sentido y al final, en la punchline, aparece el segundo. No se traduce palabra por palabra: el chiste está en el inglés. Para explicarlo, localiza la palabra clave, di sus dos sentidos y muestra por qué encajan en la escena. Muchos puns provocan más un quejido que una carcajada, y eso forma parte del juego.
Preparación + palabra con dos sentidos + remate:

formula.texto: I used to be a banker,

nota.es: preparación: sugiere el mundo del dinero
giro: prepara el remate
palabra clave con dos sentidos: interés bancario y ganas

titulo.es: Sincero o sarcástico: busca las pistas

texto.es: El sarcasmo usa palabras positivas para criticar o burlarse («Thanks a lot!» cuando alguien te estropea algo). Tres pistas lo delatan: la voz (plana, alargada, con suspiro), el contexto (la situación contradice lo dicho) y el contraste entre palabras y gesto. Con audio sintético la voz no ayuda, así que fíjate en el contexto y en lo que se cuenta. Cuidado: so + adjetivo y such a + nombre intensifican tanto un elogio sincero como uno sarcástico: «You are so kind» puede ser verdad o burla.
Palabra positiva + pista + situación mala = sarcasmo:

nota.es: palabra positiva exagerada
pista de tono: suspiro o voz plana
contexto: la situación contradice las palabras

titulo.es: Exagerar con gracia y sin herir

texto.es: La hipérbole exagera a propósito para hacer reír: nadie cree que la maleta pese un millón de kilos. Para intensificar usa so + adjetivo + that + resultado absurdo, o such a + adjetivo + nombre + that. Los correlativos reparten la queja: both… and (los dos), either… or (uno u otro), neither… nor (ninguno; el verbo va en afirmativo). Para no ofender, bromea sobre la situación o sobre ti mismo y añade un suavizador: kind of, sort of, I am only joking.

nota.es: that + resultado exagerado
correlativo: neither… nor con verbo afirmativo

texto.es: En muchos contextos del inglés, sobre todo el británico y el profesional, se evita el «no» directo. Se usan frases amables que funcionan como rechazo o desacuerdo: «That might be difficult», «I will think about it», «We must have lunch sometime», «With respect…». Las pistas: modales de duda (might, could), minimizadores (a bit, slightly) y la ausencia de fecha o alternativa. No es falsedad, es cortesía; en español un «no puedo» directo suele ser más aceptable. Es una tendencia: el contexto manda.

minimizador: «un poco difícil»
sin fecha ni alternativa: no hay compromiso

texto.es: Las afirmaciones absolutas («All people here are rude») casi nunca son ciertas y pueden ofender. Para generalizar con cuidado el inglés ofrece: tend to + verbo base («People tend to be punctual»); marcadores de «en general» al inicio (by and large, as a rule, on the whole); it is not unusual for + sujeto + to + verbo; y cuantificadores como many, most o some en lugar de all. Diferencia con el español: para «soler» el inglés no tiene un verbo idéntico; se usa tend to o usually (y used to, solo para hábitos del pasado), y tend to va seguido de un verbo base.

nota.es: marcador: «en general»
sujeto: un grupo, no «todos»
tendencia: «suelen»; con sujeto plural, sin -s

In my family, Sunday lunch is a custom that we have had for many years. By and large, relatives tend to arrive around noon, and a visitor is always welcome to join us. For example, last week my cousin brought a friend from Japan, and we simply added one more chair. We usually share one big dish from the centre of the table. In some countries people eat from separate plates, whereas in mine we like to pass the food around. Neither way is better; each tradition makes sense at home. It may seem unusual at first, but visitors quickly feel at home because everybody talks, laughs and asks questions. I hope you will join us one Sunday, and I promise to explain every custom with a smile.

texto.es: Para explicar una costumbre a alguien de fuera: 1) presenta qué es y cuándo ocurre; 2) generaliza con cuidado (tend to, by and large: no todos, no siempre); 3) da un ejemplo concreto (for example); 4) compara sin juzgar con whereas, in some countries… o neither way is better. Evita «we are right / you are strange». Si algo puede sorprender, avísalo: «It may seem unusual at first». En español a veces decimos «eso es raro»; en inglés suena mejor different.

titulo.es: Recibir a un invitado sin choques

texto.es: Recibir a un invitado extranjero combina tres habilidades. Primero, da la bienvenida y explica tus costumbres con matices (We tend to…, By and large…). Segundo, si hay un malentendido, aclara sin culpar: Let me clarify…, We did not mean to…, I apologise for… Tercero, ante una pregunta incómoda, reconócela con calidez (Good question!), responde con honestidad amable y evita «siempre» y «nunca». El objetivo no es tener razón, sino que el invitado se sienta a gusto (feel at home).

texto.es: En un debate bien construido el hablante primero reconoce un punto del otro lado (concesión): Admittedly…, I concede that…, That is a valid point. Después da un giro con but, yet, even so o nevertheless y defiende su postura (refutación). Al final cierra con To conclude… Conceder no es rendirse: hace que tu refutación suene justa. Al escuchar, busca la palabra de giro: lo anterior es la concesión y lo posterior es lo que el hablante realmente defiende.
Concesión + giro + refutación + conclusión:

titulo.es: Por mucho que… y por muy… que…

texto.es: Además de although tienes tres estructuras concesivas más precisas: Much as + sujeto + verbo («por mucho que»), However + adjetivo + sujeto + verbo («por muy… que») y adjetivo + as/though + sujeto + verbo («aunque sea…»). En inglés no hay subjuntivo: el verbo va en presente o pasado normal. El adjetivo va delante, el sujeto va antes del verbo (nada de inversión) y la segunda parte no lleva but.

texto.es: Para seguir un debate escuchado, busca tres piezas. La tesis (claim) es lo que el hablante defiende: My claim is… La evidencia son datos que se pueden comprobar: a survey, figures, According to… Una opinión («I think…») no es evidencia. La objeción (objection) es el argumento contrario y la réplica (rebuttal) responde a ella. Recuerda que evidence es incontable: se dice the evidence shows, nunca evidences.
Tesis + evidencia + objeción + réplica:

nota.es: tesis: lo que defiendes
evidencia: dato comprobable
objeción: la postura contraria
réplica: respuesta a la objeción

In my view, pupils should clean their classroom once a week. Admittedly, it takes time away from lessons, and some parents will say that cleaning is the job of the school. That is a reasonable point, but what matters is the habit we build. It is the pupils who use the room every day, and it is undoubtedly fairer that all of us look after it. Arguably, a clean room also helps us study better, because nobody likes to work among rubbish. Another reason is the cost: it is the cost of extra staff that the school would pay otherwise, and that money could buy books instead. Clearly, ten minutes on Friday is not too much to ask. To conclude, what is essential is that we share the work, because the classroom belongs to all of us.

texto.es: Para rebatir sin sonar agresivo, concede primero y luego combina tres recursos. Atenúa lo que no puedes probar con arguably o it seems that; refuerza lo que sí sostienes con undoubtedly, clearly o essential; y destaca lo importante con una frase hendida: What matters is… («lo que importa es…») o It is the cost that… («es el coste lo que…»). No mezcles atenuación y refuerzo en la misma afirmación, y recuerda que tras It is + elemento va that, no what.

items.respuesta: In my view, pupils should clean their classroom once a week. Admittedly, it takes time away from lessons, and some parents will say that cleaning is the job of the school. That is a reasonable point, but what matters is the habit we build. It is the pupils who use the room every day, and it is undoubtedly fairer that all of us look after it. Arguably, a clean room also helps us study better, because nobody likes to work among rubbish. Another reason is the cost: it is the cost of extra staff that the school would pay otherwise, and that money could buy books instead. Clearly, ten minutes on Friday is not too much to ask. To conclude, what is essential is that we share the work, because the classroom belongs to all of us.

titulo.es: Debate vecinal: todo el bloque junto

texto.es: En un debate vecinal encadenas lo aprendido en el bloque: tesis (My position is that…), dos argumentos con evidencia (First…, According to…), una concesión (Admittedly…, Much as I…) seguida de una refutación (nevertheless, what matters is…, it is… that…) y una conclusión (To conclude…). Varía el tono con arguably y undoubtedly. Escucha primero qué concede el otro: así sabrás cuál es su verdadera objeción y podrás responderla con precisión.

explicacion.es: Para lamentar algo pasado el inglés exige had + participio; el español usa el pretérito y por eso se cuela explained.

texto.es: Salvar la cara (save face) es darle a otra persona una salida digna tras un error o un comentario brusco. En inglés se consigue quitando peso al error (It's easily done, No harm done), asumiendo parte del problema (I may not have been clear) o suponiendo buena intención (I'm sure you didn't mean it that way). Para lamentar algo propio del pasado usa wish / if only + had + participio: I wish I had explained it better. Nunca empieces por you always / you never.

titulo.es: Dejar la puerta abierta sin prometer

texto.es: Cuando no puedes o no quieres decir ni sí ni no todavía, el inglés cortés usa respuestas que no comprometen: I'll bear that in mind («lo tendré en cuenta»), Let me get back to you («ya te respondo»), I can't promise anything, It depends on… Dejan la puerta abierta sin mentir: no dices «sí», dices «aún no lo sé». Así mantienes la relación y ganas tiempo. Cuidado con la gramática: bear that in mind, depends on, y con can't promise el resto va en positivo: anything, no nothing.

texto.es: Los comunicados diplomáticos dicen cosas duras con palabras suaves. We note with concern equivale a «estamos preocupados y queremos que cambie»; frank discussions, a «discutimos con dureza»; we regret, a «lamentamos lo ocurrido y nos afecta»; we remain committed to…, a «seguimos dispuestos, pero no hay acuerdo». Lately, the kitchen has been a bit of a mess in the evenings, and the music has been loud after eleven. I am sure you do not notice it, and I do not want to blame anyone. I wish you would wash your dishes on the same day, and if only the walls were thicker, I would not need to mention the music. titulo.es: Mediar en la reunión del piso

texto.es: Mediar es dirigir con tacto: dar turno, resumir lo dicho y cerrar con un acuerdo. Combina lo visto en el bloque: la queja suave (I wish you would…, If only…), las peticiones y preguntas indirectas (I was wondering if…, Could I ask whether…?), las preguntas reportadas (Mia asked whether…) y las fórmulas para reconocer al otro y no comprometerse antes de tiempo. Antes de acordar, resume qué ha dicho cada uno; al final, cierra con una pregunta de acuerdo: Are we all happy with that?

explicacion.es: En inglés el adjetivo va antes del sustantivo; en español «crecimiento rápido» lo pone detrás.

texto.es: Los textos académicos prefieren sustantivos a verbos. En vez de «Cities grew rapidly» escriben «the rapid growth of cities»: el verbo (grow, adopt, reduce) o el adjetivo (aware, efficient) pasa a ser sustantivo (growth, adoption, reduction, awareness, efficiency), el adverbio se vuelve adjetivo (rapidly → rapid) y el sujeto original va detrás de of. Así una oración entera cabe en un bloque que sirve de sujeto de otra frase. Al leer, busca el sustantivo y pregúntate qué verbo o adjetivo había detrás.
Oración verbal → bloque nominal + verbo nuevo:

nota.es: oración original: sujeto + verbo + adverbio
verbo grow → sustantivo growth; el adverbio pasa a adjetivo
el sujeto original va después de of
el bloque nominal ya es sujeto de una frase nueva

texto.es: Para juzgar un estudio, el inglés académico usa adjetivos que dicen cuánta confianza merece. texto.es: Un abstract resume un estudio en un orden fijo: objetivo (aim: qué se quería averiguar), método (quién, cuántos, cuánto tiempo), resultados (qué se encontró, con cifras) y conclusión (qué significa y qué límites tiene). According to the study, the new bike lanes have led to a rapid growth in cycling and a reduction in car traffic. The lead researcher argues that the investment has already paid for itself, and she points out that shop sales along the lanes have risen. Critics claim, however, that the results for small shops are unreliable. She acknowledges this limitation and suggests repeating the survey with a larger sample.

Five years ago, the city council decided to build more than one hundred kilometres of protected bike lanes. At first, many residents were against the plan. Shop owners were especially worried, because they believed that fewer parking places would mean fewer customers. However, the figures published this spring tell a different story. The number of people who cycle to work has risen from three per cent to eleven per cent, and car traffic in the centre has fallen by nine per cent. Air quality has also improved, and the noise in the main streets has decreased. Several schools have reported that more pupils now come to class by bicycle. The researcher who led the study argues that the investment has already paid for itself, because the city now spends less on road repairs and on health care. She points out that sales in the shops along the new lanes have grown by six per cent. Nevertheless, some critics claim that the results for small shops are unreliable, since only forty businesses answered the survey. The researcher acknowledges this limitation, and she suggests that the council should repeat the survey next year with a larger sample.

texto.es: Parafrasear es contar la idea de otra persona con tu propia estructura y tus palabras, y atribuirla siempre. El verbo de cita muestra cómo te sitúas: according to (con to) introduce una fuente neutral; argue y maintain presentan una tesis defendida; suggest es cauteloso; claim toma distancia y acknowledge admite un límite. Tras el verbo va that + oración. Para condensar, usa nominalizaciones («cycling grew» pasa a «the growth in cycling») y no atribuyas dos veces: According to… y argue juntos sobran.
Fuente + verbo de cita + that + idea condensada:

nota.es: atribución neutral: «según…»
verbo de cita + that + oración
nominalización que condensa «cycling grew»
idea parafraseada con tus palabras

The study shows a rise in cycling and a decrease in traffic after the city built bike lanes. The researcher maintains that the project has paid for itself, and she notes that shops along the lanes sell more. Some critics claim that the information about small businesses is incomplete, and she acknowledges that a larger survey is needed next year.
items.texto: Five years ago, the city council decided to build more than one hundred kilometres of protected bike lanes. At first, many residents were against the plan. Shop owners were especially worried, because they believed that fewer parking places would mean fewer customers. However, the figures published this spring tell a different story. The number of people who cycle to work has risen from three per cent to eleven per cent, and car traffic in the centre has fallen by nine per cent. Air quality has also improved, and the noise in the main streets has decreased. Several schools have reported that more pupils now come to class by bicycle. The researcher who led the study argues that the investment has already paid for itself, because the city now spends less on road repairs and on health care. She points out that sales in the shops along the new lanes have grown by six per cent. Nevertheless, some critics claim that the results for small shops are unreliable, since only forty businesses answered the survey. The researcher acknowledges this limitation, and she suggests that the council should repeat the survey next year with a larger sample.

The aim of this study was to examine whether daily walking improves memory. Briefly, two hundred adults were followed for six weeks, and half of them walked thirty minutes a day. Overall, the people who walked scored eight per cent higher on a memory test. It is often assumed that exercise helps memory, and these findings suggest a modest benefit. However, all the participants were volunteers, so it is difficult to generalise the results to everyone. To answer your question, we cannot say that exercise improves memory for all people. Further research is needed, and for now the conclusion is tentative.

titulo.es: Resumir un estudio: pasiva impersonal y cautela

texto.es: Al resumir un estudio para tu grupo, sigue el orden objetivo, método, resultado y límite. Briefly y overall ayudan a condensar. Para presentar opiniones o hallazgos sin decir quién los sostiene, usa la pasiva impersonal: It is assumed / believed / thought that… o It has been shown that…, con el sujeto it obligatorio (en español basta «se piensa que»). Cuando alguien pregunte si se puede extender el resultado, responde con prudencia: It is difficult to generalise… y conclusión tentative.

titulo.es: Un plan de negocio: secciones y su lenguaje

texto.es: Un plan de negocio tiene secciones fijas y cada una usa su propio lenguaje. El resumen dice qué harás y para quién; el mercado describe a los clientes objetivo y a la competencia; el marketing explica cómo te darás a conocer (will + verbo); las operaciones dan horarios y turnos; las finanzas indican cuánto dinero necesitas y cuándo habrá beneficio; los riesgos nombran lo que puede salir mal, con may; y el equipo muestra la experiencia de quienes lo harán. Para reconocer una sección, fíjate en las palabras clave y en el tiempo verbal.

texto.es: El vocabulario de un pitch es preciso y suele ir con una cifra o una razón. Scope es el alcance de un proyecto; stake, la participación que alguien tiene en el negocio; leverage (verbo), sacar partido de algo que ya tienes, como contactos o una marca; margin, la diferencia entre lo que cobras y lo que cuesta; overheads, los gastos fijos; niche, un hueco de mercado pequeño y concreto; viable, que funciona en la práctica; y scale up, ampliar el negocio (sin que los costes crezcan igual). Usa cada término con un dato que lo concrete.

titulo.es: Contingencias: Should, in the event of, failing that

texto.es: Un plan de contingencia dice qué harás si algo sale mal. En registro formal se sustituye if por la inversión Should + sujeto + verbo base: Should demand fall, we will… (= If demand falls…). Otras fórmulas son in the event of + sustantivo (In the event of a delay,…) y in the event that + oración (In the event that the supplier is late,…). Failing that introduce el plan B cuando lo primero no funciona. La consecuencia debe ser una acción concreta con will (o would si es muy hipotética).

titulo.es: Presentar un plan y responder a objeciones

texto.es: Presentar un plan es un desempeño con orden fijo: apertura (saluda y di qué vas a mostrar), calendario (by + will have, will be + -ing), tareas delegadas (have / get + objeto + participio), un riesgo con su contingencia (Should… / In the event of…) y respuesta a las objeciones. Ante una objeción, reconoce la preocupación (I understand that concern), tranquiliza (let me reassure you) y responde con un dato (our forecast is…). Mantén un tono realista: promete lo que puedes cumplir y usa may o expect para lo incierto.

titulo.es: Desconfiar del narrador y deducir el pasado

texto.es: Un narrador poco fiable (unreliable) cuenta la historia de modo que no puedes creerle del todo: miente, exagera, oculta algo o solo ve una parte. Las pistas son detalles que chocan con su versión: un objeto, una fecha, otro personaje o una reacción demasiado defensiva. Para deducir qué pasó de verdad usa modal + have + participio: must have (casi seguro que ocurrió), can't have (casi seguro que no ocurrió) y might o could have (es posible). En español dirías «debió de» o «no pudo»; en inglés, el negativo de la deducción es can't, nunca mustn't.

nota.es: la pista: un detalle que contradice al narrador

titulo.es: Motivo, símbolo y tema: no son lo mismo

texto.es: Al analizar una obra distingue varios niveles. El motivo (motif) es un elemento que se repite: el agua, una puerta cerrada. El símbolo (symbol) es una cosa concreta que representa una idea: un reloj roto como tiempo perdido. El tema (theme) es la idea general que sostiene la obra: la ambición, la pérdida. El foreshadowing anticipa lo que pasará sin decirlo, y la imagery son las imágenes que crean atmósfera. Para valorar el efecto usa verbos como convey (transmitir) o resonate with (calar en el lector).
Elemento + qué representa + efecto:

nota.es: el motivo: lo que se repite en la obra
símbolo: representa una idea
la idea: el tema que apoya
el efecto: resonate with + personas

titulo.es: Leer un relato con cinco preguntas

texto.es: Para comprender un fragmento breve hazte cinco preguntas. ¿Quién lo cuenta? Primera persona (I) o tercera (she, he): eso es el punto de vista. ¿Qué quiere el protagonista? Es su motivación. ¿Cuál es la idea general? Es el tema. ¿Cómo suena el texto? Es el tono: amargo, tenso, tierno. ¿Qué no se dice pero se adivina? Eso se infiere (infer) a partir de una pista. Responde siempre con una prueba: The tone is bitter, because… / We can infer that…, because…

The Last Train is a quiet film about a woman who waits alone at an empty station every night. The plot is gripping, and the lead actor gives a convincing performance. For example, she never gets on the train, so she must have been waiting for someone special. Her calm voice also suggests that she can't have been surprised by the ending, and she might have known the truth from the start. Although the pacing is slow and the ending feels rushed, these are minor flaws in a stunning film. The cast is excellent, and the story is never predictable, so I was never bored. The music is simple, but the silence says more than any dialogue, and I was moved by the last scene. In short, it is a thoughtful film with a strong central idea. I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys slow, thoughtful stories, and I would give it four out of five.

I would argue that the ending of The Blue Door is ambiguous on purpose. The narrator says that nobody ever lived in the house, but he can't have been honest, because he also says that his sister left after an argument. The wet letter is a clue: she must have written it in a hurry, and he might have hidden it for years. In my reading, the blue door is a symbol of a memory that he cannot close. Carlos thinks the narrator is lying to us, and I concede that this is plausible. However, I am not convinced that the book wants us to be certain. The writer hides an important detail in a subtle way, and the imagery of cold and rain makes the sadness resonate with readers. It is a thoughtful novel, although the pacing is slow in the middle, and I would recommend it to anyone who enjoys a gripping story with a difficult ending. Fair enough, Carlos: we will have to agree to disagree.

texto.es: En un club de lectura se discute el significado, no hay una única respuesta. Propón tu lectura con prudencia (I would argue that…, In my reading…), defiéndela con dos deducciones apoyadas en pistas (must have, can't have, might have) y reconoce lo que te conceda el otro (You make a fair point, I concede that…). Si no te convence, dilo con tacto: I see your point, but I am not convinced. Un buen debate combina todo el bloque: pistas del narrador, vocabulario literario y valoración con ejemplos.

The cold imagery conveys sadness, and the ending will resonate with anyone who has lost someone. It is a thoughtful book, although the pacing is slow. You make a fair point, Carlos, but we will have to agree to disagree.
items.texto: Club de lectura. La novela «The Blue Door» termina así: el narrador cierra la puerta azul de la casa y dice «Nobody ever lived here». Antes contó que su hermana se fue tras una discusión y que la carta de ella apareció mojada. texto.es: La jerga (slang) es vocabulario muy informal que oirás entre amigos, en series y en redes. Para reconocerla, pregúntate dos cosas: ¿qué significa en lenguaje neutro? (I'm beat = I am very tired) y ¿dónde se puede decir? Con amigos y compañeros cercanos, sí; en una entrevista, con un cliente o en un correo formal, no. Además, parte de la jerga es regional: mate suena muy británico o australiano, y dude, más estadounidense. Reconocerla te ayuda a entender; usarla solo cuando la situación lo permite evita que suenes descortés.

texto.es: Cuando oyes una palabra desconocida en habla natural, no te detengas: sigue escuchando y busca una pista cerca. Puede ser una definición (which means…), un contraste (but, although: suele significar lo contrario), una causa o consecuencia (so, because) o ejemplos próximos (people shouting and laughing). Después deduce un significado y comprueba que encaja en toda la frase; si la frase sigue teniendo sentido, vale. No necesitas entender cada palabra para captar la idea del mensaje.

texto.es: Un diario informal combina tres capas. Primero, bloques que organizan la idea: The thing is…, To be honest…, To be fair…, It's not like… Segundo, expresiones coloquiales de la semana, con moderación: I'm beat, swamped, bummer, awesome, no worries; dos o tres bastan. Tercero, una estrategia de comunicación cuando no entiendes: Sorry, I didn't catch that / Could you rephrase that? Cuenta los hechos en pasado simple y recuerda los verbos con infinitivo: manage to, decide to, forget to.

titulo.es: Resolver un problema en inglés, sin asentir a ciegas

texto.es: Esta clase integra todo el bloque. Cuando tienes un problema en un país extranjero: plantéalo con datos (The heating isn't working), pide una acción con cortesía (Could you send someone to fix it?), y si la otra persona usa jerga que no entiendes, no asientas: repite la expresión y pregunta What do you mean by…? Después confirma con tus palabras (So, to make sure I understand, …). Para resumir la semana usa bloques (To be honest…, The thing is…) y verbos con to o -ing (manage to, avoid + -ing).

You said the heating was a bit dodgy, and sorry, I didn't catch that. What do you mean by dodgy? Could you rephrase it? So, to make sure I understand, it is unreliable and it breaks down a lot, and you will send a plumber on Friday morning. Basically, I paid a deposit last week, so I hope we can sort it out soon. texto.es: Las charlas memorables empiezan con un gancho (hook) en los primeros segundos. Cuatro aperturas muy comunes: una pregunta al público (Have you ever…?), una anécdota (Last year, I…), un dato sorprendente (Nine out of ten…) y una promesa (By the end, you will…). Tras el gancho llega una señal de organización (signpost) que anuncia el camino: Let me outline…, First…, In a moment…. Al escuchar, pregúntate qué hace cada frase: ¿engancha o anuncia la estructura?

texto.es: Las señales guían al público: First abre; Moreover añade; Having said that contrasta con lo anterior; Moving on cambia de punto; Let me recap repasa; To sum up o To conclude cierran. La pregunta retórica (Who has never…? Why does it matter?) no espera respuesta: sirve para que el público piense y se sienta incluido. Úsala tras una afirmación o un dato, y deja una breve pausa. Ojo: no combines señales que dicen lo mismo (Having said that, but…).

texto.es: Muchas charlas eficaces siguen este camino: gancho, problema, solución, regla de tres y cierre que retoma el inicio (callback). Al escuchar, localiza cada pieza por su función: el problema señala algo que va mal (The trouble is…), la solución lo arregla (Here is what works…), la regla de tres reúne tres elementos paralelos (fast, cheap and green) y el cierre vuelve a la historia del principio. Conocer la estructura te ayuda a anticipar y a no perderte.
Gancho → problema → solución → regla de tres → cierre:

Every night, millions of us do the same thing. We lie in bed, we pick up the phone, and we say, just five more minutes. But who has ever stopped after five minutes? Nobody. Never have we had so many tools to talk to each other, yet rarely do we feel rested. Not only do we lose sleep, but we also lose focus, energy and patience. Think about your last bad day at work or school. Was it the lack of ideas? Or was it the lack of sleep? Here is what I suggest: a simple plan with three rules. First, leave the phone outside your bedroom. Second, turn off the screen one hour before bed. Third, read a book instead. Little did I know that three small rules would change my mornings. Seldom have I felt so calm and so awake. So tonight, try it. Put your phone down, close your eyes and give your body the rest it needs.

Every evening, most of us repeat the same habit. We take the phone to bed and we scroll for one more minute. Why do we do it? Because it feels harmless. Never have we been so connected, yet rarely do we feel calm. Not only does the screen steal our sleep, but it also steals our focus, our energy and our patience. So I suggest three simple rules. First, charge the phone in the kitchen. Second, switch off the screen an hour before bed. Third, read a few pages of a book. Seldom have I slept so well as in the week I tried it. So tonight, try it, and tell a friend how you feel tomorrow. Is it really so hard to put a phone down? I bet it is easier than you think.

Have you ever run so slowly that a walker passed you? That was me, three years ago, on my first morning with the Park Runners club. I was a beginner, I was out of breath, and I wanted to quit. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, running is not about speed; it is about habit. Moreover, the club gave me friends who waited for me at every corner. Having said that, nobody made me feel small. Second, running changed my head: I am calmer, happier and more patient. Seldom have I felt so proud as on the day I finished my first ten kilometres. items.respuesta: Have you ever run so slowly that a walker passed you? That was me, three years ago, on my first morning with the Park Runners club. I was a beginner, I was out of breath, and I wanted to quit. Today I will tell you why I stayed. First, running is not about speed; it is about habit. Moreover, the club gave me friends who waited for me at every corner. Having said that, nobody made me feel small. Second, running changed my head: I am calmer, happier and more patient. Seldom have I felt so proud as on the day I finished my first ten kilometres. Third, it is cheap. You only need shoes and a park. To sum up, run slowly, run with friends and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the walker who passed me? Last week, I passed him. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be fast to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.

Seldom have I felt so proud as on the day I finished my first ten kilometres. Third, it is cheap. You only need shoes and a park. To sum up, run slowly, run with friends and never stop trying. That is my takeaway. And remember the walker who passed me? Last week, I passed him. Thank you for your question: you asked whether you must be fast to join. Not at all; beginners are the heart of our club.

Good evening. Nine out of ten people quit a new sport in the first month. Today I want to show you how to stay. First, choose a sport that you love. Moreover, find a club, because friends make every hour easier. Having said that, you must be patient. Second, practise a little every day. Third, enjoy the small wins. Never have I felt so happy as on the day I finished my first race. Last year, I was a beginner too, and I was afraid of looking silly. Now I look forward to every training. Why wait? Start this week, and you will see. To sum up, be patient, be kind to yourself and have fun. That is my takeaway. Good question, by the way: you asked if it is expensive. Not at all; a pair of shoes is enough.

titulo.es: Resumir lo que dijeron los demás

texto.es: Para resumir una mesa redonda, sustituye said por verbos que muestren la postura: stressed (subrayó), doubted (dudó), conceded (reconoció), insisted (insistió), warned (advirtió), suggested (sugirió), admitted (admitió), argued (sostuvo). Elige el verbo por la intención de la persona, no por cortesía: doubted no es denied. Después de that, la frase suele retroceder un tiempo (can → could, will → would). Al escuchar, pregúntate: ¿defiende, duda, avisa o propone?

Thank you, Tom. That is a valid point, and I agree with you up to a point. Phones do distract students, and nobody can deny it. But I see one drawback in a complete ban: many students use their phones to learn. For instance, last week my teacher asked us to record a short interview, and every group used a phone for it. texto.es: Moderar es estructurar, no opinar. Empieza presentando (Welcome, everyone; tonight's topic is…; Let me introduce…). Da turnos claros (Ana, would you like to start? Tom, it is your turn) y reconduce si hace falta (Sorry to cut in, but coming back to…). Resume con verbos variados (Ana stressed…, Tom doubted…) y cierra agradeciendo (To wrap up…; I am grateful to…). Un buen moderador habla poco y deja que los ponentes se oigan entre sí.

items.respuesta: Good evening, everyone, and welcome to tonight's panel. Our topic is technology in the classroom. Let me introduce our three panellists: Ana, who uses tablets every day; Tom, who teaches science; and Sara, who has three children at school. Ana, would you like to start? Thank you, Ana. Tom, it is your turn. Sorry to cut in, Tom, but coming back to the topic, could you tell us about the cost? Thank you. Before we move on, let me recap. Ana stressed that tablets saved time and made lessons more fun. Tom doubted that schools could afford them, and he warned that screens could distract students. Sara suggested that we write clear rules, and she conceded that tablets had real benefits. Sara, what would your first rule be? Seldom have I seen three guests agree on so much. To wrap up, all of you agree that rules matter more than machines. I am grateful to each panellist for a lively discussion, and I thank our audience for listening. Good night, everyone.

texto.es: Cada pregunta de entrevista busca algo distinto, aunque suene parecida. Tell me about a time… pide una experiencia real en pasado. What would you do if…? es hipotética: evalúa tu criterio. What was your motivation…? pregunta por tus razones. What is your biggest limitation? busca un punto débil y cómo lo trabajas. Could you elaborate…? pide más detalle. texto.es: En una entrevista, las preguntas indirectas suenan más corteses y dejan hablar al otro. Tras Could you tell me…, I would like to know… o I am curious…, el orden es el de una frase afirmativa: sujeto + verbo, sin did ni inversión (why you chose). Para preguntas de sí/no usa whether o if. Las preguntas de sondeo directas, en cambio, sí llevan auxiliar: To what extent did…? What precisely do you mean by…? Sirven para pedir grado, exactitud o más detalle.

texto.es: Una respuesta fuerte tiene dos piezas: un ejemplo concreto (qué hiciste, cuándo y cómo) y un resultado que se pueda contar (cifras, plazos, efectos). Last spring, I was in charge of the school recycling project. When I arrived, the bins were full because nobody had collected the paper for a week, and many students had stopped caring. My first step was to listen. I asked every class what was making recycling difficult, and most students said that nobody knew who was responsible. So I drew up a weekly rota and asked each class to choose a captain. I also wrote a short checklist for the captains, and I checked the bins myself every Friday during the first month. As a result, the bins have never been full again, and our recycling rate has doubled since then. Teachers have even started using the rota in other projects. The experience taught me that clear responsibility prevents most problems. It also taught me that a leader should listen before giving orders. Since then, I have used the same approach in every team I have joined.

When I arrived, the bins were full because nobody had collected the paper for a week, and many students had stopped caring. My first step was to listen. Two years ago, I was in charge of the charity concert at my school. When I joined the team, the posters were still not ready because nobody had booked the hall, and the students had already lost interest. I decided to start again with a clear plan. I made a checklist, I asked each class to choose a captain, and I called the music teacher to ask for help. We booked the hall within two days and sold every ticket in a week. As a result, the concert has become a yearly tradition, and the school has raised twice as much money since then. The experience taught me that a simple plan gives people confidence. I also learned that asking for help early saves time. Today, I use the same method whenever I start a new project.

texto.es: Cuando te hacen una pregunta inesperada, no hace falta responder al instante: hay frases para ganar tiempo. Las informales (Hang on, let me think; Hold on) van bien entre amigos. titulo.es: Las cuatro partes de una respuesta improvisada

texto.es: Una respuesta improvisada ordenada tiene cuatro partes. Primero el punto: tu postura en una frase (My point is that…). Después la razón: por qué piensas así (The main reason is that…). Luego un ejemplo que la apoye (For example…). Por último el cierre, que repite el punto (In conclusion…). Si te desvías, reconócelo y vuelve: Sorry, I'm rambling; let me go back to my point. Al escuchar, busca cada parte y fíjate en cuál falta.
Punto + razón + ejemplo + cierre:

nota.es: punto: tu postura
razón: por qué
ejemplo: un caso concreto
cierre: repites el punto

Let me think for a moment. I would say that specialists are better, so my stance is clear. The first reason is that experts solve hard problems faster. A specialist has spent years on one subject, and companies pay more for that skill. For example, my uncle is an engineer who only repairs bridges, and he is always busy because nobody else can do his job. Some people say a generalist is more flexible, and that is true. texto.es: En una noticia conviven tres tipos de enunciados. Un hecho se puede comprobar en un registro o una medición: The library opened in 1998. Una afirmación (claim) suena a hecho, pero aún necesita pruebas: The app doubles your speed. Una opinión es un juicio personal y no se puede comprobar: It is the best app. Las señales ayudan: the report states y according to the figures apuntan a un hecho con fuente; claims y allegedly, a algo sin probar; in my opinion, a un juicio. Ojo: evidence no tiene plural.

texto.es: Una falacia es un paso que suena convincente pero no se sostiene. Tres muy frecuentes: el falso dilema (solo dos opciones, cuando hay más), la generalización apresurada (una muestra pequeña se convierte en regla para todos) y el ataque personal (se ataca a quien habla, no a su argumento). I read the blog post about mobile phones and marks, and I think it has two important weaknesses. First, it seems to rely on a very small sample: the writer asked only five friends, so the result cannot speak for the whole school. Arguably, this is the main weakness, because five friends are not enough to prove anything. Second, the post is one-sided. It says the solution is to ban phones, but that is a false dilemma, because there are many other options. To some extent, the writer is right: the fall in marks may be linked to phones, and phones are likely to distract some students. However, a link is not proof, and other factors, such as stress or sleep, may account for the trend. A more balanced alternative would be to survey every class and then agree some simple rules, rather than ban everything. In my opinion, that would be fairer and more reasonable for everybody.

items.respuesta: I read the blog post about mobile phones and marks, and I think it has two important weaknesses. First, it seems to rely on a very small sample: the writer asked only five friends, so the result cannot speak for the whole school. Arguably, this is the main weakness, because five friends are not enough to prove anything. Second, the post is one-sided. It says the solution is to ban phones, but that is a false dilemma, because there are many other options. To some extent, the writer is right: the fall in marks may be linked to phones, and phones are likely to distract some students. However, a link is not proof, and other factors, such as stress or sleep, may account for the trend. A more balanced alternative would be to survey every class and then agree some simple rules, rather than ban everything. In my opinion, that would be fairer and more reasonable for everybody.

Arguably, that is enough to make the conclusion weak. The post also offers only two choices, ban phones or lose the marks, and that is a false dilemma. To some extent the writer has a point, because the drop in marks is likely to be linked to phones, but it could also be a coincidence, and other factors may account for it. A reasonable alternative would be to survey every class, rather than five friends, and to agree simple rules together. In my opinion, a more balanced post would be clearer and more useful.

I checked the viral story about the school closing, and I rate it as unproven. First, the post says the council has cut the budget in half, but it comes from an account with no name and gives no source, so we cannot confirm it. Second, the photo of the empty building is real, but it is misleading, because it was taken during last year's summer holidays, out of context. texto.es: Verificar es un proceso, no una opinión. Paso 1: separa las afirmaciones y evalúa cada una. Paso 2: busca la fuente original y el contexto (The photo is real, but it is misleading). texto.es: Un ensayo de cinco párrafos tiene una estructura predecible. La introducción presenta el tema y termina con la tesis: la idea que todo el texto defiende. La conclusión retoma la tesis con otras palabras (restates) y cierra sin añadir ideas nuevas. Leer la tesis y la primera frase de cada párrafo te da el esquema.

texto.es: Para no repetir palabras, el inglés escrito enlaza las frases con referencias. This/these + sustantivo resume la idea anterior (This decision…). Such a + sustantivo la califica («una decisión así»). The former y the latter distinguen dos elementos citados, el primero y el segundo; respectively los empareja en el mismo orden. texto.es: Un borrador con problemas de coherencia suele mostrar cinco síntomas. Repetición: la misma palabra abre todas las frases. Referencia ambigua: un pronombre (she, it, they) puede ser dos cosas. Salto lógico: pasas de una idea a otra sin la razón que las une. Frase irrelevante: no tiene que ver con el tema. Contradicción: una frase niega otra. Léelo como un lector que no sabe nada y pregunta en cada frase: ¿a qué se refiere?, ¿por qué esta conclusión?, ¿encaja aquí?

nota.es: Una referencia es ambiguous cuando un pronombre tiene dos candidatos posibles.

traduccion.es: Palabras vagas como «things» y «stuff» («cosas») dejan al lector sin tener claro el punto.

nota.es: Vague = impreciso; unclear = poco claro para el lector.

Last year I had to choose between staying in my hometown and studying in another city. Admittedly, staying was the easy option: my family, my friends and my job were all there. Nevertheless, I decided to leave, because I wanted to learn something new. The choice was not simple. I made a list of the advantages and the risks, and I talked to my cousin, who moved abroad two years ago. She told me that the first months are hard, but that the experience changes you. Although I was nervous, I sent my application in March, and I was accepted in June. Now I live in a small flat near the college, and I cook for myself every day. To save money, I work at weekends. Our school has a new rule about phones. The rule says phones must stay in bags. My brother plays football on Saturdays. Students who break the rule lose their phones for a day.

Should students have a say in the school rules? In this piece I will argue that they should. First, rules that nobody explains are rarely followed. When students help to write a rule, they understand the reason for it, and they respect it more. Second, taking part teaches responsibility. A student who helps to decide learns that every choice has consequences. I concede that students may not always choose the best rules. Nevertheless, teachers can guide the discussion, and, as mentioned above, a rule with a clear reason is easier to accept. This argument is stronger than the objection, because guided choices are still choices. Teachers and students want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness. A shared rule can give both. In conclusion, students deserve a voice in the rules they must follow, and the school will be calmer for it. Revision: I cut a repeated sentence and replaced due to the fact that with because.

This argument is stronger than the objection, because guided choices are still choices. Teachers and students want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness. A shared rule can give both. In conclusion, students deserve a voice in the rules they must follow, and the school will be calmer for it. Revision: I cut a repeated sentence and replaced due to the fact that with because.

Do students deserve a say in school rules? I believe they do, and in this piece I will argue it. First, a rule that nobody explains is rarely followed, so students should know why it exists. Second, helping to make rules teaches responsibility, because a student learns that choices have consequences. Admittedly, some students will not choose wisely; nevertheless, teachers can guide them, and, as mentioned above, a clear reason makes any rule easier to accept. This argument answers the objection. Teachers and students often want different things: the former want order, and the latter want fairness, and a shared rule can give both. To sum up, schools should give students a voice, and the result will be a calmer and fairer place. Revision: I changed a long sentence into a shorter one and removed a repeated word.

texto.es: Un buen lector separa lo que los datos demuestran de lo que solo sugieren. Los verbos fuertes (prove, demonstrate, show) afirman una causa; los cautos (suggest, indicate, appear to, may, could) apuntan a una relación. Que dos cosas ocurran juntas es una correlación y no prueba que una cause la otra. Después busca los límites: muestra pequeña, participantes voluntarios, un solo lugar o ausencia de grupo de comparación. Regla: la conclusión nunca debe ser más fuerte que los datos.

Our survey of two hundred pupils produced two main findings. First, sixty per cent of the pupils sleep less than eight hours a night. Second, among the pupils who sleep little, twice as many girls as boys say that they feel tired in class. These figures suggest that a lack of sleep may affect how pupils feel at school, and they appear to show that girls are more affected than boys. However, the results have an important limitation. All the pupils came from one school, and they described their own sleep, so the data may be biased. For this reason, we cannot say that sleep causes tiredness; we can only say that the two seem to be linked. Further research with a larger sample from several schools would be needed before we can speak for all teenagers. In short, the findings are interesting, but they should be read with care.

Last June a survey was conducted among three hundred residents of the old neighbourhood. The participants were selected at random from a list and were asked to complete a questionnaire online. Two results stand out. First, roughly a third of the residents said that the street lighting is poor. Second, twice as many older residents as young ones feel unsafe at night. These findings suggest that lighting may be a priority for the neighbourhood, and they appear to show that older people are more worried. However, there is an important limitation: most answers came from two streets, and the residents described their own feelings, so the data may be biased. For that reason, we cannot generalise the results to the whole city. As a next step, we propose a three-month trial of new lamps in the two streets, and we suggest that the council should report the results in the autumn. Further research with a larger sample would then show whether the change really helped.

Most of the answers came from two streets, and people only reported how they feel, so the results may not be reliable. We therefore cannot say that the same is true for the whole city. Our proposal is a trial of three months with new lamps in those streets, and we recommend that the council reports the results in the autumn. More research with a larger sample would show whether the trial helped.

texto.es: En una conversación rápida la gente se interrumpe, termina las frases de otros y habla a la vez. En los textos se marca con un guion (—): «Are we gonna book the room or— / —already did». texto.es: El inglés se habla en decenas de países y cada variedad tiene su acento, su ritmo y algunas palabras propias, aunque comparte casi toda la gramática. Aquí practicas lo que se ve en el texto: el léxico y las estructuras. Son rasgos típicos: prepone (India, «adelantar»), how far? y flash me (Nigeria), grand y «I am after + -ing» (Irlanda), arvo, reckon y heaps (Australia). Como la voz de la app es sintética, el acento lo aprenderás oyendo hablantes reales. Si no entiendes una palabra, deduce por el contexto o pide que te la aclaren.

titulo.es: Lo que se dice y lo que se quiere decir

texto.es: En inglés cotidiano, sobre todo con cortesía, lo importante suele quedar sin decir. Una pausa («Well…»), un suavizador (a bit, I suppose, hardly) o una respuesta vaga (I will think about it, we will see) suelen significar «no» o «no me convence». Estrategia: pregúntate qué esperaba el oyente y si la respuesta cumple esa expectativa; si evita decir sí o no, probablemente es un no amable. Es distinto del español, donde se suele ser más directo: «It is a bit pricey» casi nunca es solo un comentario sobre el precio.
Pausa + suavizador + respuesta vaga = rechazo amable:

nota.es: pausa: algo va a incomodar
suavizador: el «no» se disfraza de comentario

The lecturer outlined three reasons why cities are planting more trees. According to her, the first reason is that trees cool the streets, and shade can make a street up to five degrees cooler in summer. The second reason is rain: the ground near a tree takes in more water, so there is less flooding after a storm. The third reason is that trees are good for people's minds, because residents who live near trees feel less stressed. In short, trees are not a quick fix, but they are a good long-term investment.

In this episode, the host asked her guest whether it is better to work from home. According to the guest, it depends. First, many people save about two hours a day because they do not travel, and this is a real benefit. Second, some workers feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. Third, she said that companies could offer two office days a week, which she described as a good compromise. When the host asked whether working at home is better, she answered that it is not exactly better, which seemed to imply that the answer is not a simple yes. What struck me was that she never said it is easy. To be fair, I found the episode balanced. However, I would add one doubt: not everybody has a quiet room at home, so the benefits may be smaller for some people. I see her point, but I would like to hear more before I decide. In short, the episode was clear and useful, and I agree with her up to a point.

Host: Welcome to the show. Today my guest studies working from home. Is it better to work at home? Guest: Well, it depends. Many people save two hours a day because they do not travel, and that is a real benefit. Host: So it is better? Guest: Not exactly. Some people tell me they feel lonely, and they hardly see their colleagues. Host: Is there a solution? Guest: Perhaps. Companies could offer two office days a week, and I suppose that is a good compromise. Host: Thank you for joining us.

texto.es: Un episodio de pódcast se trabaja en cuatro pasos: 1) toma notas mientras escuchas; 2) resume con fidelidad lo que se dijo (The host asked…, According to the guest…); 3) señala la implicación, lo que se insinúa sin decirlo (seemed to imply…; «Not exactly» suele ser un no amable); 4) añade tu reacción con matiz (to be fair, I see her point, but…, I would add…, I agree up to a point). feedback.es: El texto resume lo dicho con fidelidad, detecta la implicación de «not exactly», reacciona con matiz y cierra con una conclusión.

items.respuesta: In this episode, the host asked her guest whether it is better to work from home. According to the guest, it depends. First, many people save about two hours a day because they do not travel, and this is a real benefit. Second, some workers feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. Third, she said that companies could offer two office days a week, which she described as a good compromise. When the host asked whether working at home is better, she answered that it is not exactly better, which seemed to imply that the answer is not a simple yes. What struck me was that she never said it is easy. To be fair, I found the episode balanced. However, I would add one doubt: not everybody has a quiet room at home, so the benefits may be smaller for some people. I see her point, but I would like to hear more before I decide. In short, the episode was clear and useful, and I agree with her up to a point.

On the positive side, many people save two hours a day because they do not travel to an office. On the negative side, some of them feel lonely and hardly see their colleagues. She suggested that a good compromise could be two office days a week. The host asked again whether working at home is better, and the guest replied not exactly, which implied that the situation is more complicated than a simple yes or no. My reaction is positive: to be fair, she did not try to sell one answer. What struck me was how honest she was about the problems. texto.es: Corregir sin saber por qué falla se olvida en una semana; diagnosticar el error lo fija. texto.es: Reparar es cambiar solo lo necesario. Marca el error, nombra la regla y toca únicamente las palabras que fallan: un pronombre olvidado (That film, it was brilliant), un conector que sobra (Much as I admire her, I disagree), un orden mal puesto (However expensive the ticket is…), una condición formal (Should demand fall, …), una preposición equivocada (the demand for tickets) o un tiempo que rompe la secuencia (had already left). Después relee la frase entera: si suena natural, está reparada.

titulo.es: Lo que dice la letra y lo que sugiere

texto.es: Una letra casi nunca lo dice todo. El significado literal es lo que dicen las palabras (a door); el figurado, lo que quieren decir (una promesa que no se cumple). Además, una letra puede implicar cosas que nunca nombra: una luz encendida sugiere que alguien espera. Para interpretarla: busca la metáfora, traduce la imagen a una idea, fíjate en el tono (suave, irónico, resignado) y decide qué se insinúa sin decirse. Apoya siempre tu lectura en una palabra concreta del texto.

Rain tapped the window of the bus. Leo checked his watch for the fifth time, tapping his foot on the wet floor. On his knees lay the folder with his drawings, and his hands would not stay still. The driver hummed a cheerful song, which made everything worse. Off the bus he jumped, and up the stairs he ran. Silence in the corridor. A closed door. He had missed the interview by ten minutes, and he had practised his speech for a week. Then a woman appeared at the end of the hall, holding a cup of tea. "Are you Leo?" she asked. "We had to postpone everything. The director, of course, is stuck in traffic." Leo laughed so loudly that the secretary looked up. She offered him a cup of tea, and he drank it slowly. In the end, he got the job. The director arrived an hour later, blaming the bus.

Every Sunday my grandfather used to fish at the lake, and every Sunday he came home with an empty bucket and a happy face. My mother would laugh and say that fishing was only an excuse to sit in silence. One morning I followed him. Into the water went his line, and out of the silence came nothing. Hours passed, and the lake stayed as silent as a painting. Then a tiny silver fish jumped into the bucket by itself. My grandfather stared at it. "Unbelievable," he whispered. His hands shook a little as he held the bucket. I had never seen him so excited, or so suspicious. "Of course," he said at last, "the day I bring a friend, the fish behave." In the end, he let the fish go and told everybody it was the best catch of his life. Since then, he has never fished alone.

I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. Last year, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I understand that the budget is small, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

texto.es: La simulación pide combinar lo del bloque en una sola intervención: presentas una idea con un breve contexto narrativo (Last year, the square had been empty…), la defiendes ante una objeción con concesión y tacto (Much as I appreciate…, I was wondering whether…), anticipas imprevistos (Should it rain, …) y cierras con un plan y un plazo (By Friday, we will have…). items.respuesta: I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. Last year, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. The square belongs to all of us, and a story is the cheapest way to fill it. I understand that the budget is small, and much as I appreciate your concern, I believe we can manage. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.
aceptadas: I would like to put forward a proposal for the open day: a story workshop in the square. Last year, the square had been empty for months, and many neighbours told me they missed a place to meet. A workshop with a small book stall could change that. I was wondering whether the volunteers could bring the books and the chairs, so the cost would be almost nothing, and nobody would need to spend money on anything else. Should it rain, we will move the workshop into the hall. Failing that, we can shorten the morning. If everyone agrees, I will confirm the stall by Friday, and by Saturday we will have prepared the posters. Shall we agree on that? Thank you for listening, and I hope you will join us.

Let me put forward a proposal: a story workshop for the open day. When I was a child, the square used to be full of people, and I would love to see that again. Stories can bring neighbours together, and a simple workshop is a good way to start. Nobody needs a big stage to tell a story, only a few chairs and a little time. Fair enough, the budget is limited. Much as I would like a bigger stall, I am sure the volunteers can help, and I was wondering whether the library could lend us some books for the morning. In the event of rain, the workshop will take place in the hall. By Friday I will have confirmed the stall with the council, and the posters will be ready by Saturday. That is our deadline, and I am confident that we can meet it together. Are we all happy with this plan?

titulo.es: Leer un artículo de opinión como analista

texto.es: Para analizar un texto largo de opinión no lo leas solo para entenderlo: interrógalo. ¿Cuál es la tesis, la afirmación central? ¿Qué postura muestran los verbos y las cautelas (I would argue, tend to)? ¿Dónde concede el autor un punto antes de rebatirlo? ¿Qué recurso usa (una pregunta retórica, un contraste, un ejemplo)? Y, sobre todo, ¿qué implica sin decirlo? Localiza cada respuesta en una frase concreta del texto: sin evidencia, tu análisis es solo una opinión.

titulo.es: Editar con precisión, capa por capa

texto.es: Editar con precisión es revisar por capas y elegir siempre el cambio mínimo. Mira (1) los tiempos: ¿qué pasó antes?; (2) el registro: ¿a quién escribes?; (3) la cohesión: ¿a qué se refieren this y such?; (4) los conectores: ¿suman, contrastan o dan resultado?; y (5) la concisión: ¿sobra algo? Ante cada marca, nombra la capa, decide el arreglo más pequeño y relee la frase completa para comprobar que el tono sigue siendo el tuyo.

texto.es: Valorar una actuación modelo es aplicar criterios, no dar una impresión. Usa una rúbrica de cuatro: estructura (apertura, razones, cierre), precisión (tiempos, conectores, orden), tacto (concesión, peticiones suaves, contingencias) y evidencia (datos y ejemplos). I would argue that the centre should be car-free on Sundays. For example, the air is cleaner and children can play safely. Much as some shops may lose customers, the change is worth trying. So, all in all, it deserves a chance.

I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.

aceptadas: I would argue that schools should limit phones in class, but not ban them completely. For example, in my cousin's school the students keep their phones in a box during lessons, and the teachers say that the pupils now listen more carefully. Admittedly, phones can be useful: a dictionary, a map or a camera can help with a project. Much as I respect that view, the evidence I have seen points to another conclusion, because when a phone is on the desk, it is hard to ignore. The benefits depend on rules, or rather, on clear rules that everyone understands. What I mean is that the problem is not the phone itself but the moment when it is used. Schools could allow phones for specific tasks and keep them away during explanations and exams. Some parents worry about emergencies, so the school office should always be available by telephone. On balance, a limited and well-explained rule would help pupils to concentrate without feeling punished.

In my opinion, phones should stay in the bag during lessons. Take my own class: last year, we used to check messages all the time, and the teacher had to repeat every explanation twice. It is true that phones can help with research, and I do not want a total ban. Even though a quick search can save time, it also opens a hundred distractions. To put it more precisely, a phone is useful only when the teacher asks for it. Let me rephrase that: a phone is a tool, not a toy, and a tool needs a purpose. For instance, the class could use phones for a short quiz and then put them away. That is a fair compromise. Some students may feel nervous without their phones, but they would soon notice how much they can concentrate. All in all, a clear and limited rule is better than a total ban or complete freedom. Students need trust, and they also need help.

Admittedly, an app alone may not be enough: it cannot give you a real conversation. Much as I respect the author, I would argue that the claim is too strong. The source seems to rely on a small survey, and it gives no data about students who also talk with people, so its conclusion may not be reliable. When I was a child, I would watch films in English without understanding a word, and my cousin used to laugh at me. Later, I had to take an exam, and that was the moment when I decided to learn properly. An online post claims that apps are a waste of time. It is true that an app cannot replace a teacher. Even though I agree with part of that view, I think the post may be wrong, because it gives no numbers and does not say who wrote it. The source seems weak, so I would be careful before believing it. I was wondering whether the author has ever used an app for a full year. With respect, one experience does not prove a rule. I appreciate that some people learn better with a teacher, and I see your point. Let me rephrase my conclusion: apps do not teach everything, but they help you to start. In the end, I changed my opinion only a little, and this course helped me to explain why.
